action_criteria.label: Obtain tissue by maximal safe resection of the left parietal lesion, or stereotactic biopsy if resection is not safely feasible, for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis with IDH1 R132H immunohistochemistry, IDH1/IDH2 sequencing, ATRX immunohistochemistry, BRAF V600E and MGMT promoter methylation
action_criteria.rationale: Surgery is the first option for a resectable glioma and should be as extensive as safely possible (AIOM; EANO 2021). Only tissue establishes the integrated diagnosis and the molecular results that select treatment; IDH sequencing is added because he is under 55 (EANO 2021), and BRAF V600E separates a giant-cell-rich glioblastoma from pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma and identifies a targetable alteration (van den Bent 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Dexamethasone can blunt amlodipine's blood pressure control and raise glucose; levetiracetam has no interaction with dexamethasone
action_criteria.label: Check interactions of dexamethasone and his levetiracetam with his amlodipine

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform lumbar puncture: 6 mm midline shift with subfalcine herniation and papilledema carries a risk of herniation
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide, alkylating chemotherapy) before tissue diagnosis is established
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given upcoming neurosurgical intervention and bleeding risk
required_recommendations: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for maximal safe resection of the left parietal lesion, with preoperative functional MRI and DTI tractography and intraoperative mapping; send the specimen for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis (WHO CNS5).

Start dexamethasone for symptomatic vasogenic oedema (for example 4 mg every 6 to 8 hours after a loading dose when mass effect is marked) at the lowest effective dose, with glucose monitoring and gastric protection, and taper after surgery.

Continue levetiracetam for the generalized tonic-clonic seizure nine months ago, now recognised as tumour-related epilepsy; this is treatment, not prophylaxis. Review the dose (500 mg twice daily is a low maintenance dose) and increase it if seizures recur. Avoid enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital), which lower dexamethasone and chemotherapy exposure.

After the integrated diagnosis and recovery from surgery, refer to the neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team and choose treatment on the post-operative KPS (now 60, depressed by mass effect): for glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, MGMT unmethylated, radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide if KPS recovers to 70 or more (Stupp 2005; EANO 2021), or hypofractionated radiotherapy 40 Gy in 15 fractions alone if KPS stays below 70 (EANO 2021); a clinical trial is reasonable given the unmethylated MGMT promoter.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Arjun Mehta is a 52-year-old right-handed man who presents with a two-day history of progressively worsening holocranial headache, multiple episodes of projectile non-bilious vomiting, and new-onset right-sided weakness. His wife reports that approximately nine months ago, he experienced a single generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home, for which he was evaluated at an outside hospital. At that time, a non-contrast head CT reportedly showed a subtle ill-defined hyperdense area in the left high parietal region, and a diagnosis of viral encephalitis was made. He was treated with a two-week course of intravenous acyclovir and started on levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily as antiseizure treatment. He initially improved and returned to his baseline functional status. Over the past several weeks, his wife has noticed progressive cognitive slowing, with him taking longer to complete routine work tasks and occasionally struggling to find the right words during conversations. Two days prior to presentation, he developed a severe holocranial headache that was unresponsive to acetaminophen. The headache was described as constant, pressure-like, and worst in the early morning hours. The following day he had three episodes of projectile vomiting without nausea. On the morning of presentation, his wife noticed that he was having difficulty lifting his right arm and was dragging his right leg while walking. She also observed a subtle droop on the right side of his face. There has been no fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, visual changes, or bowel or bladder incontinence. He denies recent travel, sick contacts, or known exposures. He has no history of malignancy, weight loss, night sweats, or chronic cough. He was brought to the emergency department by his wife and subsequently admitted for urgent neurological evaluation and imaging.
